problemText: Which of the following is a signal word that usually shows a cause/effect pattern in an informational text?
choices: unlike
because
first
solved this by
hints: Signal words point to the pattern. Which word links one event to a result it produces?
Cause/effect shows why one event makes another happen.

problemText: Read this short text: 'Paragraph 1: The school library had a problem — the tables were old and wobbly, and students did not feel safe using them. Paragraph 2: The librarian asked the principal for new tables, and the principal approved the purchase. Paragraph 3: After the new tables arrived, students started spending more time in the library.' What is the organizational pattern of this text?
choices: Chronological, because the events happen one after another in time
Cause/effect, because the wobbly tables caused students to stay away
Problem/solution, because it names a trouble and then explains how it was fixed
Compare/contrast, because it shows the library before and after the purchase
hints: Look for a real trouble that needs to be named first, then a fix that solves it.
The key signal words are 'had a problem' and the approval of new tables.

problemText: A text about how to make a clay pot includes these paragraphs in order: first gathering the clay, then shaping it on a wheel, next letting it dry, and finally firing it in a kiln. Why is chronological order the right pattern for this topic?
choices: Because the topic is solving a problem by listing all the equipment needed to make pottery in the workshop
Because the topic is comparing different ways to make pottery using wheels versus hand-shaping methods
Because the topic is explaining why clay shrinks when it dries out during the kiln-firing stage
Because the topic requires showing the steps in the exact order they must happen
hints: Think about what the topic itself needs. Can you skip steps or do them out of order?
Directions and real processes need events to happen in a particular sequence.

problemText: Read this text: 'Paragraph 1: A hurricane brings heavy rain and high winds to a coast. Paragraph 2: The heavy rain causes flooding in low-lying areas because water has nowhere to go. Paragraph 3: The high winds cause damage to buildings and trees, which then blocks roads and power lines. Paragraph 4: As a result, people lose their homes and power for weeks after the storm.' A student says this text is chronological because it describes events happening during a hurricane. Explain what the student got wrong and name the correct pattern.
choices: The student missed that even though events happen in time, the text is really showing cause/effect because each paragraph explains how one event makes another event happen.

The student confused the topic with the pattern; while hurricanes occur in time, this text is problem/solution because it identifies a weather disaster and then describes ways people prepare to stay safe.
The student overlooked that this is compare/contrast because the text separates the heavy rain damage from the high wind damage and shows how they differ from each other.
The student misread the signal words; the text is actually chronological only for the first half, then switches to cause/effect in the second half, so it uses a mixed pattern overall.
hints: Look at the connecting words: 'causes,' 'because,' 'as a result.' What do these words signal about how the paragraphs connect?
A text can move through time without being chronological. The pattern depends on whether paragraphs just list events or show one event making another happen.

problemText: Two students read a text about how a town planted trees to reduce flooding during heavy storms. Student A says the pattern is problem/solution. Student B says the pattern is before-and-after compare/contrast, since it shows the town before the trees and after the trees. Using what you know about organizational patterns and how they fit their topics, explain which student is correct and why.
choices: Student B is correct, because whenever a text describes conditions at one point in time and then describes conditions at a later point in time, that structure automatically qualifies as a compare/contrast pattern.

Student A is correct, because the text names a real trouble (flooding) and explains the fix (planting trees). Before-and-after is not automatically compare/contrast if a fix is what caused the change.
Both students are correct because the text could be read either way depending on which paragraphs you focus on and how you interpret the author's main purpose.
Neither student is correct, because this text is actually chronological order since it follows the events in sequence through time rather than presenting two separate subjects to examine.
hints: Remember the trap: a before-and-after description is not automatically compare/contrast. Check whether the text names two separate things to weigh against each other.
A pattern fits its topic for a reason. Does this topic call for weighing two separate things, or for explaining how a problem was solved?

problemText: Read this text: 'Paragraph 1: Frogs and toads both have bumpy skin and lay eggs in water, but they are different in many ways. Paragraph 2: Toads have thick, dry bumps and live mostly on land, while frogs have smooth, wet skin and spend most of their lives in water. Paragraph 3: Because toads live on land, they need to come to water only to breed, so they can survive in places where water is scarce. Paragraph 4: Frogs, however, must stay near water or moisture all the time because their skin dries out easily.' Now choose the statement that names the pattern correctly and explains both what makes that pattern fit and what could make a student get confused.
choices: Cause/effect, because the repeated use of connecting words such as 'because' and 'so' in multiple paragraphs signals that the text is showing why one thing happens as a result of another rather than weighing two items.
Chronological order, because the text describes how both animals developed their unique traits over time and explains the sequence of their evolution from a common ancestor.

Compare/contrast, because it sets frogs and toads side by side to show how they are alike and different, even though some paragraphs use 'because' and 'so' which might make a student think the text is cause/effect.
Problem/solution, because the text identifies the challenge that each animal faces in finding appropriate habitats and presents the physical adaptations as the solution to that challenge.
hints: The whole text's job is to set two separate creatures side by side and show how they differ. That is compare/contrast. But look at those connecting words—why might they fool a reader into seeing a different pattern?
A text can use signal words from more than one pattern. The key is to ask: what is the main job of the whole text? Is it to weigh two things, or to show why one thing causes another?

problemText: An author's purpose is the reason a text was written. Which of the following is a purpose that an author might have for writing an informational text?
choices: To describe what the author had for breakfast
To make the reader laugh at a joke
To explain facts and give information about a topic
To tell a made-up story about imaginary characters
hints: Remember the three main purposes: to inform, to persuade, or to entertain.
Informing means sharing facts and explanations without pushing the reader to believe or do anything.

problemText: Read these two sentences about a new library rule. Sentence 1: 'The library now closes at 6 p.m. instead of 8 p.m. on weeknights.' Sentence 2: 'Students should visit the library right after school, before the new closing time ruins your study plans.' Which sentence contains word choice that signals the author is trying to persuade rather than just inform?
choices: Sentence 1, because it uses the word 'now' to signal that a change has happened and readers need to know about it
Sentence 2, because it mentions the library and students who need to access it during school hours
Sentence 1, because it gives a specific time of day when the library will close to the public
Sentence 2, because it includes the word 'should' and describes the closing time negatively as something that 'ruins' plans
hints: Look for words that judge something or tell the reader what to do.
Neutral words like 'closes at' just report what happens, but words like 'should' and 'ruins' ask the reader to feel or act a certain way.

problemText: A local newspaper published two articles about the same community garden project. Article A lists the garden's location, watering schedule, and types of vegetables that will grow there. Article B describes only the beautiful flowers the garden will produce and ends with 'Join us this Saturday to help make our neighborhood bloom.' Which article's purpose is to persuade, and what word choice proves it?
choices: Article B persuades, proven by the call to action 'Join us this Saturday' and the word 'bloom' used to make the garden sound appealing
Article A persuades, proven by listing the specific vegetables that grow in the garden and providing a detailed watering schedule
Article A persuades, proven by telling readers the exact location of the garden so they know where to find it
Article B persuades, proven by describing flowers instead of focusing on the vegetables that the garden will produce
hints: Persuading means pushing the reader toward an action or belief—look for judgment words or commands.
A sentence that asks readers to actually do something is a clear signal of persuasion.

problemText: A student wrote a passage about adopting shelter dogs. The passage includes: the number of dogs at the local shelter, details about how friendly and healthy the shelter dogs are, statements that 'every family deserves the joy of a pet,' and it ends with 'Please contact the shelter this week.' Which statement best explains why the selected details and word choice reveal the author's purpose?
choices: The passage informs because it includes a specific number of dogs at the shelter, which is a factual detail that provides readers with objective information without judgment
The passage persuades because it selects details that make shelter dogs sound worthy of adoption and uses the judgment word 'deserves' plus a call to action, pushing the reader toward a choice
The passage informs because it selects only positive details about shelter dogs, which helps readers understand the shelter's mission in a factual and straightforward way
The passage persuades because it mentions that the local shelter exists and includes contact information that allows readers to take immediate action on behalf of the shelter
hints: An informing passage would report outcomes or details from more than one side; a persuading passage lines up details that all point toward one side.
Look at both the selected details AND the word choice together—'deserves' is a judgment, and 'Please contact' is a direct call to action.

problemText: Two texts describe the school's new homework policy. Text X states only the facts: homework is due by Friday, it counts toward the semester grade, and late homework receives half credit. Text Y states that homework deadlines have been set at Friday and late homework gets half credit, but then adds, 'Students who turn work in late are cheating themselves out of learning time.' Which best explains the difference in the authors' purposes?
choices: Text X persuades and Text Y informs because Text Y provides more facts about the late homework credit policy and explains the reasoning behind it
Text X persuades and Text Y informs because Text X includes information about how homework affects the semester grade, which is a factual detail most readers need
Text X informs and Text Y persuades because Text X reports plain facts while Text Y adds a judgment that late work is a form of self-harm, pushing readers to meet the deadline
Text X informs and Text Y informs because both texts describe the same homework deadline and credit system using similar language and tone
hints: The same topic can have different purposes depending on word choice and selected details.
A judgment statement like 'cheating themselves out of learning time' signals persuasion, while plain facts without judgment signal informing.

problemText: A school newsletter includes a section titled 'Parking Lot Safety Update.' It reports: 'Three vehicles backed into parked cars in the lot this month. Two drivers did not see the parked cars because they were not paying attention. One accident involved a student who was standing nearby.' The section ends with 'All drivers should slow down and check mirrors before backing up.' Explain what the author's purpose is and point to the exact proof from both word choice AND selected details.
choices: The author informs because the section includes facts about how many accidents happened this month and describes specific incidents with exact numbers and causes
The author persuades because the section mentions a student standing in the parking lot during one of the accidents, which makes readers worry about safety
The author informs because the section lists the number of vehicles involved in the accidents and explains in detail that drivers were not paying attention to their surroundings
The author persuades because the section selects only examples of problems caused by careless driving and ends with 'should slow down,' a command asking drivers to change their behavior
hints: An informing passage about an event would describe both good and bad outcomes, or explain why something happened without taking a stance; a persuading passage picks details that all point toward one view and ends with what readers should do.
Look at both what details were selected AND what words were chosen—'should' is a command, and all three examples make careless driving look bad.

problemText: Two accounts describe a school assembly held on Tuesday afternoon. Both accounts state that the assembly lasted one hour and was held in the gymnasium. Account A also mentions that the principal gave a speech about good citizenship. Account B mentions that student council members helped set up chairs before the event. Which statement best explains what a shared fact is?
choices: A detail that appears in both accounts and describes part of the event itself, not one writer's special addition
A detail that one writer noticed but the other writer missed by accident because they were not paying close attention during the event
A detail that makes one account more interesting or longer than the other account by including extra information one person observed
A detail that both writers must have learned from the same source or document before they each wrote their own separate account
hints: Look back at the definition: shared facts are on BOTH lists and are part of the event itself.
Think about the assembly example: what did both accounts say exactly the same way?

problemText: Two accounts describe the same baseball game on Friday evening. Source A (a fan's social media post) says: 'Our team won 7-4, and watching my best friend hit a home run in the third inning made the whole night perfect.' Source B (the local sports section) says: 'The home team defeated the visiting team 7-4 in front of 340 fans. The winning pitcher struck out eight batters.' Both accounts describe the same game. Which detail appears only in Source B and not in Source A?
choices: The game ended with a score of 7-4
The winning pitcher struck out eight batters
The home team won the game
A player hit a home run in the third inning
hints: Review both sources carefully and list what facts appear in only one of them.
The correct answer is a fact about pitching statistics that appears in one source but is completely absent from the other.

problemText: Two accounts describe the same science fair held on Saturday at a community center. Source A (a teacher's message to families) includes: 'Our students presented projects on weather, plants, and the water cycle. Many projects used colorful posters, and I was proud to see how hard our class had worked.' Source B (the community center's event announcement) includes: 'The science fair ran from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Judging ended at 1:30 p.m., and three students won blue ribbons for outstanding projects.' Do these two accounts describe the same event? Explain how you know.
choices: No, because Source A talks about projects while Source B talks about prizes, so they are not about the same fair
No, because Source A describes feelings and Source B describes only facts, so they cannot be the same event
Yes, because both accounts mention a science fair with student projects, though they describe different details about it
Yes, but only if you assume the fair at the community center is the only one that happened that week
hints: Before comparing anything, check: do both accounts describe the same place, day, and type of event?
Remember, different details and different stance do not mean the accounts describe different events.

problemText:
Read the two accounts of a community garden planting day.

Source A (a volunteer's email): 'We planted thirty seedlings in the community garden on Saturday morning, working side by side with people from three different neighborhoods. Seeing everyone dig in the soil together and chat about their gardens made me feel hopeful that our community could really come together.'

Source B (the city parks department's report): 'The community garden planting event took place Saturday morning. Volunteers planted thirty seedlings in prepared beds. The department provided tools, soil, and water access. An estimated 45 people attended the event.'

Both accounts describe the same planting day. What is one shared fact that both sources state?
choices: The volunteers felt hopeful about community cooperation
Forty-five people attended the event
The city parks department provided tools and water
Thirty seedlings were planted on Saturday morning
hints: Look for a fact that appears in BOTH accounts stated in nearly the same way.
Shared facts describe what actually happened at the event, not how it felt or who organized it.

problemText:
Read the two accounts of a middle school talent show.

Source A (a student's journal entry): 'The talent show was tonight, and I sat in the audience watching my classmates perform. Three students did comedy sketches that made the whole gym laugh so hard people were crying. My friend sang a solo that gave me chills.'

Source B (the school's monthly bulletin): 'The sixth-grade talent show was held Tuesday evening in the gymnasium. Thirty-two students performed, and the show lasted ninety minutes. Five performances were comedy acts.'

Both accounts describe the same talent show. Which statement best describes how these two accounts differ in what they choose to include?
choices: Source A focuses on feelings and reactions, while Source B focuses on numbers and facts about the event
Source A is accurate because it mentions specific performers, while Source B is incomplete because it only uses numbers
Source A leaves out information on purpose to make the talent show sound better, while Source B reports only what really happened
Source A and Source B disagree because one says comedy sketches happened and the other says five comedy acts happened
hints: Notice what each source spent the most words describing—feelings and moments, or counts and logistics?
Differences in emphasis and stance are not disagreements; look for what each writer chose to include and why.

problemText:
Read two accounts of a school fundraiser book fair.

Source A (a parent volunteer's note to other parents): 'The book fair ran all week in the library, and students could buy books during lunch and after school. My child spent an hour on Thursday picking through the mystery and fantasy shelves, and she came home with four books she had been wanting. It was wonderful to see her so excited about reading.'

Source B (the librarian's fact sheet): 'The book fair ran Monday through Friday in the school library. Vendors brought a total of 2,400 books. Students were allowed to shop during lunch, after school, and during study hall. The fair earned $840 in school fund revenue.'

Both accounts describe the same book fair. Identify one fact both accounts state and one detail that appears in only one account. Then explain whether the two accounts actually disagree or simply include different details.
choices: Shared fact: students shopped during lunch and after school. Source A adds the student bought four books; Source B adds vendors brought 2,400 books. They disagree because Source B's total number contradicts Source A's small purchase.

Shared fact: the fair ran all week in the library. Source A adds how excited the student felt; Source B adds total book count and money earned. They do not disagree because both can be true of the same fair.

Shared fact: it was a book fair in the school. Source A emphasizes one child's happiness; Source B emphasizes the total revenue. They disagree because Source A focuses on reading while Source B focuses on money.
Shared fact: the fair lasted one week. Source A adds that children picked books; Source B adds the revenue amount. They disagree because one account is personal and the other is official.
hints: First, identify the detail both accounts definitely state the same way—same day, same place, same timeframe.
Second, check whether the additions on each account's special list contradict each other or sit side by side without touching.

problemText: A reason is part of an argument. Which of these is a reason? Remember: a reason explains why a claim should be believed.
choices: Three out of four teachers voted to extend lunch by ten minutes, which shows that most staff members support the change.
The cafeteria should serve healthier lunches instead of the current menu options.
Students enjoy playing basketball at recess because it is fun and keeps them active during the break.
Walking to school every day is good exercise because it strengthens your heart and legs.
hints: A reason comes after 'because' or 'since' — it answers the 'why' question.
Look for a sentence that explains a cause or consequence, not just a fact standing alone.

problemText: Read this claim and the sentence right after it: 'Our town needs more public parks. Parks give people a safe place to exercise and spend time with their families.' Does the text support this claim with a reason and evidence, or does it just state the claim and move on?
choices: The claim is supported because the next sentence gives a reason why parks matter.
The claim is not supported because it does not say which specific park should be built.
The claim is supported only if most people in town already agree with it.
The claim is not supported because no number or count is provided.
hints: To be supported, a claim needs a reason attached to it — check the sentence right after the claim.
You do not need a specific plan or a vote count for support; you just need to find a reason the text gives.

problemText: Read this sentence from an argument: 'Breakfast is obviously the most important meal of the day.' The sentence uses the word 'obviously.' Does this word count as evidence that supports the claim?
choices: Yes, because 'obviously' is a confident word that shows the writer believes the claim.
No, because 'obviously' is just confident wording, not a reason or a fact.
Yes, because when a word is printed in the text, it serves as evidence.
No, because the word 'obviously' is only three syllables long.
hints: Confident words and tone are not the same thing as reasons and facts.
Ask yourself: does 'obviously' explain why breakfast is important, or does it just sound sure of itself?

problemText: An argument states: 'The school library should stay open after 4 PM on Wednesdays. Most students have sports or clubs right after school, so they cannot use the library until later. Three students surveyed last month said they would use the library if it stayed open until 6 PM.' The argument also includes: 'An after-school library would bring our school into the modern world.' Sort these two specific claims: the one about students having sports or clubs, and the one about bringing the school into the modern world. Which is supported and which is not?
choices: Both claims are supported because they both appear in the same argument.
The modern-world claim is supported; the sports-and-clubs claim is not supported.
The sports-and-clubs claim is supported; the modern-world claim is not supported.
Both claims are not supported because no poll of the entire school was taken.
hints: For each claim, look at the sentences right around it and ask: is there a reason and a fact printed in the text?
One claim has an explanation and an actual count; the other uses confident wording with nothing backing it up.

problemText: A student reads this argument: 'The school should ban phones during lunch. When students have phones at the table, they text their friends instead of talking to the people sitting next to them. A study found that students who eat lunch without phones reported feeling more connected to their classmates.' Later, the argument says: 'Phones at lunch are just bad for you.' The student wants to sort each claim. Which statement correctly identifies whether each of these two claims is supported or not?
choices: Both claims are supported because they each relate to the main topic of phones affecting student behavior and social interaction.
Neither claim is supported because the argument does not include enough specific details about when and where the study was conducted.
The claim about phones being 'just bad' is supported by common sense; the texting claim is not supported by any real evidence.
The claim about texting instead of talking is supported by a reason; the claim that phones are 'just bad' is not supported.
hints: One claim has an explanation of cause and effect plus a research result; the other uses vague language with nothing concrete beside it.
You do not need to know whether the study is strong — just whether a reason and evidence are printed in the text.

problemText: An argument reads: 'Students should be allowed to eat lunch outside on nice days. Eating outside would give students fresh air and sunshine. Fresh air and sunshine help people feel less stressed and more alert. Being less stressed also makes it easier for students to focus on learning in their afternoon classes. Eating outside is an exciting option.' The student sorting this argument finds four specific claims: (1) eating outside would give students fresh air and sunshine, (2) fresh air and sunshine help people feel less stressed and more alert, (3) being less stressed makes it easier to focus on learning, and (4) eating outside is an exciting option. Which of these specific claims are supported by a reason and evidence found in the text, and which are not?
choices: Claims 1, 2, and 3 are supported; claim 4 is not supported.
Claims 1 and 4 are supported; claims 2 and 3 are not supported.
All four claims are supported because they are all mentioned in the same paragraph.
Only claim 1 is supported; claims 2, 3, and 4 are not supported.
hints: Trace from each claim through the next sentence or two: does the text give a reason why the claim is true, or does it just move to a new idea?
Notice that some claims receive their support from earlier claims in the chain — if a sentence in the text explains why something is true, that counts as support.
